svg.title: DDIA 6 · PARTITIONING (SHARDING): sketchnote
svg.text: When data or write load is too big for one machine, split it. Each record belongs to exactly one partition.
By key range: sorted, like encyclopedia volumes
By hash of key: even spread
✓ range scans ✗ timestamp keys → all of today's writes hit the LAST partition
✓ even load ✗ range scans hit ALL partitions (Cassandra: hash partition key, sort by clustering key)
Hash: hash(key) spreads keys evenly, so load is uniform. You
lose range queries on the key.
The cost moves to reads, which must fetch all 100 sub-keys
and merge. Only do this for keys you know are hot, and track
Global: the index itself is partitioned by term.
REBALANCING: NEVER USE HASH MOD N
A new node steals a few whole partitions from each existing
node. Used by Elasticsearch, Kafka, Riak, and Couchbase.
With few nodes, arcs are uneven. Virtual nodes place each
server at many points so load evens out, and a bigger server
The map itself lives in a coordination service (ZooKeeper,
etcd, KRaft), and routers or clients watch it for changes.
Name the shard key from the hottest query: "hash(user_id), because every hot query filters by user". Then name the cost: cross-user queries scatter.
"What about the celebrity or hot hotel?"
Key splitting with a suffix, write buffering in Redis or Kafka, and a cache in front for reads.
Pre-split into many logical partitions (e.g., 1024) mapped to few physical nodes, or consistent hashing. Never mod N.
A single Postgres handles ~10–50k TPS and multiple TB. Shard only when the calculation says one primary can't take the write load.
Study notes on Designing Data-Intensive Applications (Kleppmann). Read the book.
